threads.thread_goal: Align on current customer journey and main pain points across channels.

messages.text: Hi team, let's kick off by mapping how customers experience us right now across store, contact centre, and field sales. I'd like each of you to share one or two key pain points you see in your channel—things that slow us down or frustrate customers. This will feed into T1 and help us shape the playbook. Please share by EOD tomorrow.

Good timing. In field sales, I see we're losing time because account managers and specialised sellers don't have a shared visit structure. We end up repeating questions or missing follow-ups. Also, customers ask about promotions and we sometimes give conflicting info depending on who they talk to. I'll map out the current journey from my side and identify the gaps.

From the store side, cleanliness and display consistency are big ones. We're doing it, but there's no standard checklist, so each shift does it differently. Also, when customers have complaints about products or refunds, we don't always know the right answer—sometimes we tell them to call the contact centre, sometimes we try to handle it ourselves. Causes confusion.

Agreed on the refunds and complaints piece. In my role as specialised seller, I see customers get frustrated when they don't know who to ask. Store staff, account managers, contact centre—we all handle it slightly differently. And the follow-up after a sale is spotty. Some customers get a call, some don't. Let me document what I'm seeing and add it to the journey map.

From contact centre, the main issue is we don't always know what's happening in stores or with account managers. A customer calls about a promotion and we're not sure if it's still active. We also get escalations that could have been handled in-store if the staff had the right info. And our call scripts don't match how field sales or stores talk to customers.

I'll add the crop production side. We see issues with how products are displayed and communicated. Sometimes customers don't understand what they're buying because the info isn't clear. And when there's a complaint about product quality, we don't have a standard way to log it or follow up. I'll pull together what I'm seeing.

I'll contribute from account management. The challenge is we don't have a standard visit script, so each visit is different. And follow-up is inconsistent—sometimes we document next steps, sometimes we don't. Also, when we're in the field, we don't always have access to what the contact centre or stores have promised the customer. Creates misalignment.

Following up on my earlier note—I've started mapping the current journey. The key touchpoints are: initial contact (store or field), needs discovery, proposal, and follow-up. Right now, each channel does this differently. I'll have a draft diagram by tomorrow morning that shows where the gaps are. Should help us see what needs to be standardised.

I've been thinking about the checklist piece. If we create a simple daily checklist for store cleanliness and display, we could make it part of the opening routine. Shouldn't take more than 5 minutes. That would solve a lot of the inconsistency. I can draft something and get feedback from the team.

On the refunds and complaints—I think we need a single-page guide that all channels can use. Store staff, contact centre, account managers—everyone follows the same rules. That would eliminate the confusion. I can help draft that once we agree on the core rules.

Good points all around. Let me summarise what I'm hearing as the top pain points: (1) inconsistent refunds and complaints handling across channels, (2) no standard visit or interaction script, (3) poor follow-up consistency, (4) store display and cleanliness not standardised. Does that capture it? If so, these are the four we should prioritise in the playbook.

Yes, that's it. And I'd add that the journey map needs to show where each channel hands off to the next. Right now, that handoff is unclear. If we map it clearly, we can design the playbook to make those transitions smooth.

Agreed. The handoff is key. For example, when a customer calls the contact centre after visiting a store, we need to know what happened in the store. And when an account manager visits, they need to know if there are open issues from previous contact centre calls. That's the missing link.

I've pulled together some notes on product communication issues. Customers often don't understand the difference between product lines or what they're paying for. If we standardise how we describe products across channels, that would help. I'll add this to the journey map.

I'll work on documenting the current account management process. Right now, it's mostly ad hoc. Once I have that, we can see where it overlaps with store and contact centre processes and where we need to align.

Okay, so we have D1 locked: the four pain points are refunds/complaints, visit scripts, follow-up consistency, and store standards. For D2, I need the journey map from 394531 and 49060 by tomorrow EOD so we can confirm the high-level flow. Once we have that, we move to TH2 to design the playbook structure.
I'll have the field sales journey map ready by tomorrow morning. Should show the discovery, proposal, and follow-up steps, plus where we hand off to stores or contact centre.
And I'll get the store-side journey documented—from customer entry through purchase and follow-up. Will include where we need to escalate to contact centre or account manager.
I'll add the specialised seller perspective to the store journey. We see things from a different angle and it'll help round out the picture.

Perfect. So to confirm D1 and D2: we're prioritising refunds/complaints consistency, visit scripts, follow-up standardisation, and store display/cleanliness. The journey map will show the full customer flow across all channels and where handoffs happen. That's our foundation for the playbook. Everyone good?
Yes, that works. I'll make sure the crop production side is represented in the journey map so we don't miss anything.

threads.thread_goal: Define the structure and core behaviours of the unified playbook.

messages.text: Now that we have the journey map, let's design the playbook structure. I've drafted an outline for A1 with sections for store, contact centre, and field sales. Each section covers greeting, needs analysis, proposal, and closing. I'd like feedback on whether this structure works and what core behaviours we should emphasise across all channels. Please review and comment.

I like the structure. But I think we need to be clear about tone of voice across all channels. Right now, store staff are casual, contact centre is formal, and account managers are somewhere in between. If we standardise the tone—say, friendly but professional—that would help customers feel like they're dealing with the same company. I can draft some examples of how that would sound in each channel.

The structure looks good. For field sales, I'd suggest we add a section on how to handle objections and how to close the conversation. Also, we need to be clear about what account managers can commit to versus what needs to go back to the store or contact centre. That's been a source of confusion.

For the store section, I think we should include a subsection on how to handle customer complaints and when to escalate. Right now, staff don't know if they should try to solve it or call the contact centre. If we give them clear rules, they'll feel more confident.

Good point on tone. Let me add that to the outline. So we're looking at: greeting, needs analysis, proposal, closing, and tone of voice as the core sections. For core behaviours, I'm thinking: (1) listen actively to customer needs, (2) be honest about what we can deliver, (3) follow up on commitments, (4) escalate when needed. Does that feel right?

Yes, those four behaviours work. I'd maybe add a fifth: 'treat every customer interaction as an opportunity to build trust.' That's the underlying principle that ties the others together. And it applies across all channels.

I think the structure is solid. For account management, I'd want to make sure we have a clear template for documenting what we discuss and what the next steps are. Right now, I sometimes forget to write things down and then I'm not sure what I promised.
That's covered in T5—the field sales visit script and follow-up template. We'll make sure there's a simple form to document commitments and next steps. That ties into the playbook.

From the crop production side, I think the playbook should include a section on how to communicate product features and benefits. Customers often don't understand what they're buying. If we standardise how we describe products, that would help across all channels.

Good catch. I'll add a section on product communication to the playbook. That's part of the needs analysis step—understanding what the customer is looking for and explaining how our products meet that need.

I'm good with those four core behaviours plus the trust-building principle. That gives us a solid foundation. Now, for D3, I think we should approve the main sections: greeting, needs analysis, product communication, proposal, closing, and tone of voice. And D4 is the five core behaviours. Should we lock those in?

Yes, let's lock D3 and D4. So the playbook structure is: greeting, needs analysis, product communication, proposal, closing, and tone of voice. Core behaviours: (1) listen actively, (2) be honest about what we can deliver, (3) follow up on commitments, (4) escalate when needed, (5) treat every interaction as an opportunity to build trust. Everyone agree?

Agreed. Now we need to flesh out each section with specific guidance for store, contact centre, and field sales. I can draft the store section if you want. Should include how to greet customers, how to identify their needs, and when to escalate.

Perfect. I'll draft the contact centre section. 394531, can you draft the field sales section? And 200631, can you review all three and make sure the tone and behaviours are consistent across channels?
I'll draft the field sales section. I'll make sure it includes the visit script structure and how to document next steps. Should have it ready by tomorrow.

I'll review all three sections and make sure the tone and core behaviours are consistent. I'll also add examples of how each behaviour looks in practice for each channel. That'll help staff understand what we're asking for.

Great. So to recap: D3 and D4 are locked. Next steps: I'll draft contact centre section, 394531 drafts field sales section, 45990 drafts store section, and 200631 reviews for consistency. All by tomorrow EOD. Then we move to TH3 to tackle the checklist, refunds policy, and job aids.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on in-store checklist, refunds policy, and job aids content.

messages.text: I've drafted a simple in-store checklist for A2 that covers displays, stock levels, and cleanliness. It's designed to take about 5 minutes to complete and can be done on paper or in a spreadsheet. I've included zones so staff can check them off as they go. Please review and let me know if anything is missing or if it's too detailed.

I've reviewed the checklist and it looks good. One thing I'd add: a section for 'customer-facing issues'—like if a customer points out something broken or dirty. That way, staff know to log it and escalate if needed. Also, I think we should include a line for 'who completed the check' and 'time' so we can track it.
Good ideas. I'll add the customer-facing issues section and the tracking fields. That way, we can see if there are patterns in what's breaking or getting dirty, and we can address them.

The checklist looks practical. From the crop production side, I'd suggest adding a section on product freshness or expiry dates. That's something customers care about and it's easy to miss if we don't have a standard check.
Absolutely. I'll add a section for checking expiry dates and product freshness. That's important for customer trust.
The checklist is looking solid. Now, let's move to the refunds and complaints policy. I know 200631 was going to draft something. Can you share what you have?

I've drafted A6 with a simple policy for refunds and complaints. The key rules are: (1) store staff can approve refunds up to a certain amount without escalation, (2) contact centre can do the same, (3) anything above that goes to a manager, (4) all complaints are logged in A5 for tracking. I've included examples of typical cases so staff know how to apply the rules.
Good structure. What's the refund amount threshold you're proposing? And how do we make sure the contact centre and stores are aligned on what counts as a complaint versus a simple request?

I've set the threshold at 50 units of currency for store and contact centre staff to approve without escalation. Above that, it goes to a manager. For complaints, I've defined it as any situation where the customer is unhappy with the product or service. That includes quality issues, delivery problems, or service failures. I've added examples to make it clear.

That threshold makes sense. From the field sales side, I'd want to make sure account managers have the same authority. If I'm in the field and a customer has an issue, I should be able to approve a refund up to that amount without having to call back to the office.
Good point. I'll add account managers to the policy so they have the same authority as store and contact centre staff. That way, everyone can handle issues consistently in the field.

I like the policy. One thing I'd add: a section on how to handle complaints about staff behaviour. Sometimes customers complain about how they were treated, not about the product. We need to know how to respond to that.
Good catch. I'll add a section on service complaints. The rule would be: acknowledge the issue, apologise, and escalate to a manager for resolution. We want to make sure the customer feels heard.

Okay, so D6 is the refunds and complaints policy with the 50-unit threshold for all frontline staff, clear definitions of complaints, and a process for service complaints. Does everyone agree with that?

Yes, that works. Now, for the job aids—A7. I think we should create simple one-page cards for each role that summarise the core behaviours and key steps. Store staff get a card on how to greet and identify needs. Contact centre gets a card on call flow. Account managers get a card on visit structure. That kind of thing.

I like that approach. The cards should be visual and easy to remember. Maybe with icons or colours to make them stand out. And they should fit in a pocket or be posted near a desk. I can draft the store version.
Good. I'll draft the contact centre job aid. 394531, can you draft the account manager version? And 200631, can you review all three for consistency and make sure they align with the playbook?
I'll draft the account manager job aid. I'll focus on the visit structure, how to identify needs, and how to document next steps. Should be simple and actionable.
I'll review all three job aids and make sure they're consistent with the playbook and with each other. I'll also add examples of what good looks like for each role.

Perfect. So to recap TH3: D5 is the final checklist with customer-facing issues, tracking fields, and expiry date checks. D6 is the refunds and complaints policy with the 50-unit threshold and service complaint process. Next steps: 45990 finalises the checklist, 200631 finalises the refunds policy, I draft contact centre job aid, 394531 drafts account manager job aid, and 200631 reviews all job aids. All by tomorrow EOD.
Got it. I'll have the final checklist ready by tomorrow morning. It'll include all the feedback we discussed.
I'll have the refunds policy and job aid reviews done by tomorrow EOD. This is coming together well.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot, training sessions, and feedback collection approach.

messages.text: Now that we have the playbook, checklists, and policies drafted, let's plan the pilot and training. I'm proposing we run a two-week pilot with one store location and two account managers. We'll use A5 to collect feedback and then adjust before full rollout. For training, I'm thinking short 30-minute sessions per role, scheduled during shifts. Let me know your thoughts.

Two weeks is good for a pilot. For account managers, I'd suggest we pick one who's been with us longer and one who's newer. That way, we can see if the script and process work for different experience levels. And 30 minutes is tight for training, but if we keep it focused on the job aids and key behaviours, it should work.

For the store, I'd suggest we pick a location that's reasonably busy but not our busiest. That way, we can test the checklist and processes without overwhelming the team. And 30 minutes works for store staff—we can do it during a shift change or a quiet period.

I think we should also include a specialised seller in the pilot. That way, we can test how the playbook works when multiple roles are involved in a customer interaction. And for training, I'd suggest we do a quick walkthrough of the job aids and then a role-play scenario so people can practice.

Good idea on including a specialised seller. And role-play is a good way to make training stick. Okay, so for D7, I'm proposing: one mid-level store location, two account managers (one experienced, one newer), one specialised seller from that store, and one contact centre agent. Does that work?
That sounds reasonable. I can help identify which account managers would be good for the pilot. One experienced and one newer makes sense for testing.

For the feedback collection, I think we should use A5 but also do a quick debrief with the pilot group after the two weeks. That way, we can get both quantitative data and qualitative feedback on what worked and what didn't.
Good point. I'll schedule a debrief session for the end of the pilot week. We'll review the feedback log and discuss what adjustments we need to make before full rollout.

Now, for D8, I'm proposing: training sessions scheduled for next week, one per role, 30 minutes each, with job aid walkthrough and role-play. Weekly reporting using A8 to track complaints, compliments, and adoption. Does that work?

I like that. For the weekly reporting, I'd suggest we track: number of complaints, number of compliments, number of times the checklist was used, and number of times the refunds policy was applied. That'll give us a sense of adoption and impact.

Perfect. So D8 is locked: training next week, 30 minutes per role, job aid walkthrough and role-play. Weekly reporting on complaints, compliments, checklist usage, and refunds policy application. Pilot runs for two weeks, then we debrief and adjust before full rollout.
I'll coordinate with the account managers on their availability for training and the pilot. Should have that sorted by tomorrow.
I'll coordinate with the store location and make sure they're ready for the pilot. I'll also make sure the checklist is printed and ready to use.

Great. So next steps: D7 and D8 are locked. I'll schedule the training sessions for next week. 394531, coordinate with account managers. 45990, coordinate with the store. 200631, prepare the feedback log template and weekly reporting sheet. 24573, help with the debrief planning. Everyone good?
I'll have the feedback log and weekly reporting sheet ready by tomorrow. That way, we can start collecting data as soon as the pilot kicks off.
I'll help with the debrief planning. We should make sure we capture what worked, what didn't, and what adjustments we need to make.

Perfect. So to recap the full project: we've mapped the customer journey, designed the playbook, created checklists and policies, and now we're planning the pilot and training. After the pilot, we'll adjust and then roll out to all locations. We're on track for the 21-day deadline. Let's keep the momentum going.
